extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and informed general readers of political science and history interested in party machines and urban politics
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter excerpt analysing the causes, revenue sources, methods, and geographic extension of political 'rings' and 'bosses' (party machines) in American cities; explains why and where bossism flourishes and gives historical examples. Intended to inform readers about structural conditions that produce machine politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: I. Public subscriptions (campaign fund)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first is public subscriptions. For important elections such as the biennial elections of State officers, or perhaps for that of the State legislature, a 'campaign fund' is raised by an appeal to wealthy members of the party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So strong is party feeling that many respond, even though they suspect the men who compose the Ring, disapprove its methods, and have no great liking for the candidates. Used for important elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: II. Private contributions from wealthy men and corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions are sometimes privately obtained from rich men and especially from corporations (though statutes are now attempting to prevent this) who, though not directly connected with the Ring, may expect something from its action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: contractors seeking city work, railroad men preventing hostile legislation. This source is only available for important elections; its incidental mischief is enabling wealth to control a legislature through a Ring.

rubrics_metrics.name: III. Surreptitious appropriation from public funds
rubrics_metrics.description: An exceptionally audacious Ring has been known to make a surreptitious appropriation from the city or (more rarely) from the State treasury for the purposes not of the city or the State, but of its own election funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such appropriations are hidden from public accounts and justified by precedent, belief the other side would do the same, and expected benefits to the city. Available only when Ring officials control public funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: IV. Assessments (tax levied upon office-holders)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax used to be levied upon the office-holders of the party, varying from one to four or even five per cent upon the amount of their annual salaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and calculations given (e.g., aggregate salaries producing substantial sums). Even low-paid employees (policemen, office boys) have been assessed. Money payment does not discharge obligation to serve; forfeiture and being proclaimed 'nothing' are penalties for non-compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: V. Sale of nominations and offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Another useful expedient might seem to have been borrowed from European monarchies in the sale of nominations and occasionally of offices themselves. A person seeking nomination is often required to contribute to the election fund a sum proportioned to the importance of the place he seeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported price ranges (e.g., nominations for legislature $500–$1000, judgeships higher), effect that salaries may be raised so incumbents can bear the charge, and that amounts realized are collected and expended by small executive committees who keep no accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a Spoils System
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a Spoils System (= paid offices given and taken away for party reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as one of the principal conditions producing rings and bosses; the factor varies by place (offices better paid in some cities), and is most potent where offices and revenues are large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunities for illicit gains from possession of office
rubrics_metrics.description: Opportunities for illicit gains arising out of the possession of office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices that give facilities for lucrative jobbing or control of revenues increase temptation; unpaid officers may still abuse facilities. This is cited as a key condition producing bossdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a mass of ignorant and pliable voters
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a mass of ignorant and pliable voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, easily-led electorates in great cities make organization and manipulation easier; immigrant populations and a high ratio of politically incompetent newcomers increase susceptibility to machine control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient participation of 'good citizens' in politics
rubrics_metrics.description: The insufficient participation in politics of the 'good citizens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When respectable, capable citizens are engrossed in business and do not devote continuous attention to political work, professional politicians and machines fill the vacuum; this reduces effective opposition to rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and size correlation: rings flourish in great cities
rubrics_metrics.description: All of the four conditions above named are most fully present in great cities; therefore ring-and-bossdom is most fully developed in large urban centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, Pittsburgh, Minneapolis, St. Paul, St. Louis, Cincinnati, San Francisco, New Orleans. In second-rank cities the phenomena exist but on a smaller scale; in small towns or rural districts the dangerous conditions are reduced to a minimum.

rubrics_metrics.name: City character and population composition affect susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of the city and its character (e.g., manufacturing population, immigrant composition) affect how fully the system develops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small towns with a large manufacturing population are better fields for rings than homogeneous mercantile centres; cities with large immigrant populations or many irresponsible followers are more prone to bossism; local differences can make otherwise-similar cities vary widely (e.g., Minneapolis vs St. Paul).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rings' methods: exclusion of good citizens and use of 'workers' and disreputable elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Ring exists it can always exclude from office a good citizen known to be hostile to it; the Ring mobilizes an army of 'workers,' including disreputable elements, to secure discipline and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rings may combine keepers of tippling shops, 'bummers', and vagabonds who 'live by politics' to levy blackmail, stuff ballot-boxes, buy votes, 'repeat', etc.; leaders tolerate or use these elements because their enmity would defeat political ambitions.
